method: Union of the 45 Darwin claims with the highest composite validation score (data-test verdict × confidence, + model truth score, + mean assessor overall) and every claim id named in claim-sources/darwin-origin/lean/DarwinLaws/*.lean. Classes: A faithful precise mathematical statement; B model-dependent formalization (model named); C not a mathematical proposition. lean_status 'formalized' means a 'formalized' entry in lean/reports; truth scores and data verdicts never promote a claim.

candidates.label: Selection can independently produce similar organs in distantly related beings
candidates.note: Historical statement that convergence has occurred (electric organs); no derivation from premises.

candidates.label: Oceanic islands have fewer species than equal continental areas
candidates.model: MacArthur–Wilson immigration–extinction equilibrium with immigration decreasing in distance
candidates.note: Equilibrium richness below pool and decreasing in distance at equal area. No speciation; equilibrium assumed.
candidates.latex: I(P - S) = E S \iff S^* = \frac{P I}{I + E};\quad E > 0 \Rightarrow S^* < P;\ \partial S^*/\partial I > 0,\ \partial S^*/\partial E < 0;\quad d_1 < d_2 \Rightarrow S^*(I(d_2)) < S^*(I(d_1))
candidates.assumptions: MacArthur–Wilson (1963) equilibrium theory: a source pool of P > 0 species; absent species immigrate at a per-species rate I ≥ 0 that is a strictly decreasing function of distance from the source; resident species go extinct at a per-species rate E > 0 set by area; richness S is the balance point I(P − S) = E S. 'Equal continental area' is read as equal E with the continent at the near (high-immigration) limit.
candidates.lean_scope_note: Model-dependent (MacArthur–Wilson). Proves that the equilibrium richness is unique, lies strictly below the pool whenever extinction is positive, rises with immigration and falls with extinction, and that at equal area a remoter island is strictly poorer. It does not prove that islands sit at equilibrium, that immigration falls with distance (assumed), that extinction depends on area only, or anything about in-situ speciation, which the model omits. Darwin's clause that the deficit is 'not explained by physical conditions' is not represented; the theorem shows isolation suffices, not that conditions are irrelevant. The empirical support is the data test, not this proof.

candidates.label: Fossils from consecutive formations are more alike than those from remote ones
candidates.note: Given Darwin's own range-through premise (ch10-04), shared-lineage counts are weakly antitone in stratigraphic distance and intermediate faunas contain everything shared by their neighbours; purely combinatorial. Strict decay needs the Markov turnover model (B).
candidates.latex: i \le j \le k \Rightarrow F_i \cap F_k \subseteq F_j,\ |F_i \cap F_k| \le |F_i \cap F_j|,\ |F_i \cap F_k| \le |F_j \cap F_k|;\quad \text{Markov: } p^n < p^m\ (0 < p < 1,\ m < n)
candidates.assumptions: Range-through model: each lineage occupies a single stage interval [first, last] (darwin1859-ch10-04), the fauna of a stage is the set of lineages covering it, and similarity between two stages is the number of shared lineages. For the strict version: each lineage persists across a stage boundary independently with constant probability 0 < p < 1 (Markov turnover), and expected similarity k stages apart is p^k.
candidates.lean_scope_note: Proves (1) intermediacy: any lineage common to two stages is present in every stage between them, so the intermediate fauna is intermediate; (2) decay: shared-lineage counts are weakly antitone in stratigraphic distance, a purely combinatorial fact needing no rates; (3) under the constant-rate Markov idealisation the expected similarity strictly decreases with separation. The combinatorial part is faithful to Darwin's wording provided 'closely related' means 'shares lineages', which the data test also uses (Jaccard-type similarity on PBDB genera). It does not address morphological relatedness of non-shared lineages, and the weak inequality allows plateaus; strictness is model-dependent. The range-through assumption is Darwin's own ch10-04 and is not proved.

candidates.label: Oceanic islands have a very high proportion of endemic species
candidates.model: two-state Markov chain per lineage (divergence rate σ, replacement rate m decreasing in distance)
candidates.note: Stationary endemic fraction σ/(σ+m) rises with isolation. 'Very high' is not quantified; model built ad hoc.
candidates.latex: \sigma(1 - \pi) = m \pi \iff \pi^* = \frac{\sigma}{\sigma + m};\quad m_1 < m_2 \Rightarrow \pi^*(m_2) < \pi^*(m_1);\quad d_1 < d_2 \Rightarrow \pi^*(m(d_1)) < \pi^*(m(d_2))
candidates.assumptions: Each resident lineage is a two-state Markov chain: a non-endemic resident diverges into an endemic species at rate σ > 0, and an endemic is replaced or genetically swamped by renewed immigration from the source at rate m ≥ 0, with m a strictly decreasing function of distance. The endemic fraction is the stationary probability of the endemic state.
candidates.lean_scope_note: Model-dependent (two-state divergence/replacement chain, built for this claim rather than taken from the literature). Proves that the stationary endemic fraction is σ/(σ + m), falls strictly as replacement rises, and so is higher on remoter islands. It does not prove 'very high' or 'extremely large relative to area' (no quantitative threshold), does not treat extinction of endemics without replacement, time since colonisation, or the 'often' in Darwin's wording; the stationary distribution may not be reached. The relation of m to immigration is assumed, not derived from darwin1859-ch12-04's I.

candidates.label: Species of the same continent or sea are related despite differing stations
candidates.note: Empirical biogeographic pattern (regional affinity across habitats).

candidates.label: Succession by generation has never been broken by a world-wide cataclysm
candidates.note: Historical negative existential (no world-wide cataclysm); its logical form (unbroken descent ⇒ no total extinction) is a restatement.

candidates.label: Continents and oceanic islands were not united by land in the recent period
candidates.note: Geological-historical inference about land bridges.

candidates.label: Cave animals are related to surface fauna of their own continent
candidates.note: Prediction about affinities of cave faunas; follows from local colonisation only tautologically.

candidates.label: All domestic pigeon breeds descend from the rock-pigeon
candidates.note: Historical inference about pigeon ancestry.

candidates.label: Barriers to migration correspond closely to differences between regional biotas
candidates.model: Wright's island model of two demes exchanging migrants at rate m across the barrier, with drift for time t
candidates.note: Not yet formalized. Differentiation F_ST = 1/(1 + 4Nm) at equilibrium is strictly decreasing in m (impassability), and before equilibrium F_ST(t) increases with t (long-standing). A promising B candidate because both of Darwin's clauses map to monotonicities.
candidates.latex: F_{ST}^* = \frac{1}{1 + 4Nm},\ \partial F_{ST}^*/\partial m < 0;\quad F_{ST}(t) = F_{ST}^*\left(1 - e^{-(2m + 1/(2N))t}\right) \text{ strictly increasing in } t
candidates.assumptions: Two demes of effective size N, symmetric migration m per generation, neutral alleles, no mutation; 'difference between inhabitants' is read as genetic differentiation, not species-level turnover.

candidates.label: Each region's fossils are succeeded by allied living forms in the same region
candidates.note: Law of succession of types; empirical/historical pattern.

candidates.label: Fresh-water species range widely and allied species occur worldwide
candidates.note: Empirical statement about ranges of fresh-water taxa.

candidates.label: Physical conditions do not explain the similarity or dissimilarity of regional biotas
candidates.note: Negative empirical statement (climate does not predict biotic similarity).

candidates.label: Species of different genera and classes change at different rates
candidates.note: Empirical statement that rates differ between groups; only its consequence (more turnover at higher hazard) is provable, and is proved under ch14-07.
candidates.lean_scope_note: The claim is an empirical statement that turnover rates differ between groups (supported by the data test). The module proves only its consequence for the clock of darwin1859-ch14-07: under a constant-hazard model a higher hazard gives strictly more turnover in the same time (DarwinLaws.Succession.expectedTurnover_strictMono_in_hazard). Taking 'hazards differ' as a hypothesis would restate the claim.

candidates.label: Closer relatives tend to be closer together in time and space
candidates.model: Brownian motion of geographic position along a phylogeny (dispersal variance σ² per unit time)
candidates.note: Not yet formalized. The expected squared geographic distance between two lineages is 2σ² times their time since divergence, so it is strictly increasing in patristic distance; time proximity follows from the tree by definition. The cleanest unformalized candidate.
candidates.latex: \mathbb{E}\,\|X_i - X_j\|^2 = 2\sigma^2\, \tau_{ij},\quad \tau_{ij} = \text{time since the last common ancestor of } i, j;\ \tau_{ij} < \tau_{ik} \Rightarrow \mathbb{E}\|X_i - X_j\|^2 < \mathbb{E}\|X_i - X_k\|^2
candidates.assumptions: Lineages disperse as independent Brownian motions after splitting, with the same σ² and no barriers; 'nearer in time' is the divergence time itself. Long-distance dispersal and barriers break the model.

candidates.label: Plants of high mountains and temperate lowlands worldwide are identical or closely related
candidates.note: Empirical floristic pattern.

candidates.label: All living things share chemical composition, cell structure and laws of growth
candidates.note: Empirical statement of shared biochemistry and cell structure.

candidates.label: Trees more often have separate sexes than other plants
candidates.model: random pollen movement among the flowers of an individual (geitonogamy) versus between individuals
candidates.note: Not yet formalized. For a hermaphrodite plant bearing F flowers among a population of P plants with equal flower number, the fraction of self pollen received under uniform pollen movement is (F − 1)/(PF − 1), increasing in F; dioecy sets it to zero. Explains Darwin's reasoning, not the comparative frequency.
candidates.latex: s(F) = \frac{F - 1}{P F - 1} \text{ strictly increasing in } F \text{ for } P > 1;\quad s \to 1/P \text{ as } F \to \infty
candidates.assumptions: Pollen moves uniformly at random among all other flowers in the population; plants have equal flower numbers; the selective premise that self-pollination is harmful is taken from ch08-02.

candidates.label: Fresh-water fish species are not shared between distant continents
candidates.note: Empirical (and refuted) distributional statement.

candidates.label: Frogs, toads and newts are absent from oceanic islands
candidates.note: Empirical (and refuted) distributional statement with a dispersal-barrier explanation.

candidates.label: Northern species naturalise far more often in the south than the reverse
candidates.note: Empirical asymmetry in naturalisation (refuted).

candidates.label: Close interbreeding lowers fertility while occasional crossing raises it
candidates.model: multiplicative multilocus model with partially recessive deleterious alleles; fitness as a function of the inbreeding coefficient F
candidates.note: Not yet formalized. Mean log fitness falls linearly in F (ln W(F) = ln W(0) − B·F with inbreeding load B > 0), and an outcross resets F to 0, so crossing raises fitness. Also a candidate for Mendelian formalization alongside ch08-13.
candidates.latex: \ln \bar W(F) = \ln \bar W(0) - B F,\ B > 0;\quad F_{\text{selfing}, t} = 1 - 2^{-t} \uparrow 1;\quad F_{\text{outcross}} = 0
candidates.assumptions: Deleterious alleles at many unlinked loci with dominance h < 1/2, multiplicative fitness, random mating in the base population; 'fertility' is read as fitness. Darwin's statement is quantitative-genetic in content but model-dependent in form.

candidates.label: Instincts vary within species in a state of nature
candidates.note: Empirical statement that instincts vary.

candidates.label: Naturalised floras add proportionally more new genera than new species
candidates.model: random sampling of n colonist species from a species pool partitioned into genera
candidates.note: Not yet formalized, and weak: the natural statement compares genera gained per native genus with species gained per native species, which depends on the genus-size distribution of pool and natives. Only a conditional inequality can be derived; the data test gives supports at 0.55.
candidates.latex: \text{Species in genera of size 1 in the pool contribute a new genus per species; for pool genus sizes } s_g,\ \mathbb{E}[\#\text{new genera}] = \sum_g \left(1 - \binom{S - s_g}{n}/\binom{S}{n}\right)
candidates.assumptions: Colonists are a uniform random sample of the pool and belong to no native genus; the comparison to native ratios needs the natives' genus-size distribution as a further assumption.

candidates.label: No native terrestrial mammals on islands more than 300 miles from a continent
candidates.note: Empirical (refuted) distributional statement with a distance threshold.

candidates.label: Amount of fossil change between formations measures elapsed time
candidates.model: constant-hazard (Poisson) extinction, expected turnover 1 − e^{−μD}
candidates.note: Turnover is a strictly increasing, exactly invertible function of time at fixed μ, and increases with μ at fixed time (the 'imperfect' clause). Truth score 0.34 reflects rate variation, which the hazard theorem concedes.
candidates.latex: T(D) = 1 - e^{-\mu D};\ \mu > 0,\ D_1 < D_2 \Rightarrow T(D_1) < T(D_2);\quad D = -\frac{\log(1 - T)}{\mu};\quad \mu_1 < \mu_2 \Rightarrow T_{\mu_1}(D) < T_{\mu_2}(D)
candidates.assumptions: Constant-hazard (Poisson) extinction: each lineage goes extinct independently at a constant rate μ > 0, so the expected fraction of lineages lost over a duration D is 1 − e^{−μD}; μ is known when reading time from turnover.
candidates.lean_scope_note: Model-dependent (constant hazard). Proves that expected turnover is a strictly increasing function of elapsed time, that it inverts exactly to recover D when μ is known, and, as Darwin's 'imperfect' qualification and darwin1859-ch10-02 require, that the same elapsed time gives more turnover in a group with higher hazard, so the clock is only valid within a group of constant rate. It does not prove that extinction is Poisson, that rates are constant through time (pulsed turnover and mass extinctions violate this), or that the clock is 'fair' in practice: the truth score for this claim is low (0.34) because rates vary, which the theorem on hazard explicitly concedes rather than refutes. Expected values only; variance of the clock is not treated.

candidates.label: Distinct lineages adapted to similar conditions converge in external form
candidates.note: Historical statement about convergence and its taxonomic value.

candidates.label: Denudation of the Weald implies roughly 300 million years since the late Chalk
candidates.note: Not yet formalized. Pure arithmetic: time = distance ÷ rate. Darwin's figure of 306,662,400 years follows exactly from his stated denudation and rate; the data test refutes the premise (rate), not the arithmetic. A faithful Lean statement would prove the number from the inputs and nothing more.
candidates.latex: T = \frac{D}{v}\cdot\frac{h}{h_0};\quad D = 22\,\text{mi} = 1{,}393{,}920\,\text{in},\ v = 1\,\text{in}/\text{century for a cliff of } h_0 = 500\,\text{ft},\ h = 1100\,\text{ft} \Rightarrow T = 1{,}393{,}920 \times 100 \times \tfrac{1100}{500} = 306{,}662{,}400\ \text{yr}
candidates.assumptions: Retreat rate of one inch per century for a 500-ft cliff, scaled linearly with cliff height (Darwin's 'at this rate, on the above data'); the Weald is 22 miles across with formations averaging 1,100 ft thick (Ramsay). The product reproduces Darwin's figure exactly (checked against inputs/pg1228.txt lines 8671–8699); the data test refutes the rate, not the arithmetic.

candidates.label: Descent with modification embraces all members of each class
candidates.note: Historical inference from chains of affinities.

candidates.label: The Glacial period was simultaneous across the whole world
candidates.note: Palaeoclimatic claim about synchrony.

candidates.label: Bats occur on almost every island, often as endemic species
candidates.note: Empirical distributional statement about bats.

candidates.label: Oceans and continents have kept roughly their present positions since the Silurian
candidates.note: Geological-historical claim (refuted).

candidates.label: Sea depth between island and mainland predicts their mammalian affinity
candidates.model: isolation time increasing in channel depth (sea-level history) and divergence increasing in isolation time
candidates.note: Not yet formalized and weak: both monotonicities are premises, so the theorem is a composition of two monotone functions. Would only be worth stating together with a neutral-divergence model.
candidates.latex: t_{\text{iso}} = g(\text{depth}),\ g \uparrow;\quad d = h(t_{\text{iso}}),\ h \uparrow \Rightarrow d \text{ increasing in depth}
candidates.assumptions: Glacial low-stands expose shallow channels, so isolation time is monotone in depth; divergence (e.g. expected pairwise differences 2μt) is monotone in time.

candidates.label: Many genera are confined to one region and the most natural genera are local
candidates.note: Empirical statement about endemism of taxa.

candidates.label: Domestic dogs descend from several wild species
candidates.note: Historical inference (refuted).

candidates.label: Marine forms of life change almost simultaneously throughout the world
candidates.note: Empirical statement about synchrony of marine faunal change.

candidates.label: Groups rise gradually in species number to a maximum, then gradually decline
candidates.model: constant-rate birth–death process conditioned on eventual extinction
candidates.note: Not yet formalized; the existing Lean lemma gradual_rise_and_fall assumes the shape rather than deriving it. The expected diversity of a clade conditioned on extinction rises from 1 and falls back to 0, giving a unimodal expected trajectory.
candidates.latex: \mathbb{E}[n(t) \mid \text{extinct eventually}] \text{ rises from } 1 \text{ and tends to } 0;\ \text{unconditionally } \mathbb{E}[n(t)] = e^{(\lambda-\mu)t}
candidates.assumptions: Kendall's linear birth–death process with λ, μ > 0; the group is the lineage count; 'gradually' is the continuous-time sample-path property that n changes by ±1.
candidates.lean_scope_note: The lemma DarwinLaws.Succession.gradual_rise_and_fall takes gradualness (unit steps up and down) and the rise-peak-extinction shape as hypotheses and concludes that every intermediate species count is attained; it is a discrete intermediate-value theorem. Gradualness and the shape are the entire content of the claim (the data test returns 'mixed' precisely because many groups do not follow this curve), so a report marking the claim formalized would present the hypothesis as the proved result. Kept as a lemma, not as a formalization of this claim.

candidates.label: Animals from at most four or five progenitors, plants from as many or fewer
candidates.note: Historical inference about the number of progenitors.

candidates.label: Soft-bodied organisms and remains on non-depositing sea floor are not preserved
candidates.note: Taphonomic generalization.

candidates.label: Species and groups disappear gradually, place by place, not by global catastrophes
candidates.note: Gradual, place-by-place extinction is the empirical question (mass extinctions exist); it is the hypothesis of the existing lemmas, not a conclusion.
candidates.lean_scope_note: Gradual, non-catastrophic extinction is what the unit-step hypothesis of DarwinLaws.Succession.gradual_rise_and_fall and rarity_precedes_extinction asserts, so it cannot also be their conclusion. The spatial part ('first from one place, then another') has no representation in the module. The data test is 'mixed' (mass extinctions exist), which is the empirical question.

candidates.label: Unity of type is explained by unity of descent
candidates.note: Explanatory claim (unity of type by descent); not a proposition with a proof.

candidates.label: Hybrids vary little in the first generation but greatly in later generations
candidates.model: Mendelian inheritance at unlinked diallelic loci from two inbred (homozygous) parental lines
candidates.note: Not yet formalized. The F1 between two homozygous lines is genetically uniform (zero genetic variance), while the F2 segregates with genetic variance Σ(a²/2 + d²/4) per locus > 0; this is exactly 'little variation in the first generation, great in later ones'. Darwin's explanation (disturbed reproductive system) is wrong but the pattern is a theorem of Mendelism. Strong B candidate.
candidates.latex: \mathrm{Var}_G(F_1) = 0;\quad \mathrm{Var}_G(F_2) = \sum_{\ell} \left(\tfrac{1}{2} a_\ell^2 + \tfrac{1}{4} d_\ell^2\right) > 0 \text{ whenever some } a_\ell \ne 0 \text{ or } d_\ell \ne 0
candidates.assumptions: Parents are homozygous at every differing locus; loci are unlinked and additive across loci with within-locus effects a (additive) and d (dominance); no environmental variance in the genetic comparison; the F2 is produced by random mating or selfing of F1.

candidates.label: Species are not immutable but descend from other, mostly extinct, species
candidates.note: Historical thesis of descent.

candidates.label: Island endemics are related to species of the nearest continent
candidates.note: Empirical biogeographic rule; a dispersal-distance model would assume it.

candidates.label: Probably all organisms descend from one primordial form
candidates.note: Historical inference by analogy.

candidates.label: Overproduction makes a struggle for existence inevitable
candidates.note: Malthus' argument is itself mathematical: geometric increase versus a bounded world. Lean proves the surplus and the vanishing survival fraction. 'Struggle' is rendered only as inevitable mortality.
candidates.latex: N_t = N_0 r^t,\ r > 1:\ \forall K\ \exists t\ N_t > K;\quad \sup_t N_0 r^t \prod_{i<t} s_i \le K \Rightarrow \prod_{i<t} s_i \le \frac{K}{N_0 r^t} \to 0
candidates.assumptions: Discrete non-overlapping generations; unchecked numbers multiply by a constant r > 1 each generation from N₀ > 0 founders (Malthusian geometric increase); the area supports at most K individuals, so the realised population N₀ rᵗ ∏ sᵢ never exceeds K, where sᵢ ∈ [0,1] is the fraction of generation i's offspring that survive to breed.
candidates.lean_scope_note: Proves that geometric increase exceeds any bound, that the surplus grows without limit, and that in a bounded population the cumulative survival fraction is at most K/(N₀ rᵗ) and tends to zero, so not every generation can survive in full. 'Struggle for existence' is rendered only as inevitable mortality; competition, its forms (with conspecifics, other species, physical conditions) and its intensity are not represented. Whether any species has a constant r > 1 under unchecked conditions is empirical; Darwin's elephant calculation is not reproduced.

candidates.label: A species that has gone extinct never reappears
candidates.model: character state as a point in a continuous (or very large discrete) space evolving by a non-atomic process
candidates.note: Not yet formalized. Dollo's law as a measure-zero statement: a lineage with a continuous character distribution revisits an exact earlier state with probability zero. Used in the Lean modules as the range-through hypothesis instead.
candidates.latex: X_t \in \mathbb{R}^k \text{ with } X_t \text{ having a density for } t > 0 \Rightarrow P(X_t = x_0) = 0 \text{ for every fixed } x_0
candidates.assumptions: The identical form means identical character vector; the evolutionary process has a non-atomic marginal law (e.g. Brownian motion on characters). Says nothing about near-identical forms (iterative evolution).
candidates.lean_scope_note: The module uses this claim as its modelling assumption, not as a theorem: each lineage is given a single stratigraphic interval (DarwinLaws.Succession.Lineage, fauna), which encodes no reappearance after extinction. Darwin's argument for it (a replacement would inherit different characters from different progenitors) is about inheritance, not something provable here. Everything in the faunal-similarity results of ch10-16 and ch10-13 is conditional on it.

candidates.label: Descent with divergence and extinction produces groups subordinate to groups
candidates.note: Tree-like descent gives laminar (nested or disjoint) clades, and conversely. Divergence and extinction, which Darwin invokes for the gaps between groups, play no role in the proof.
candidates.latex: \text{TreeLike}:\ u \le w \wedge v \le w \Rightarrow u \le v \vee v \le u;\quad C(v) = \{w : v \le w\};\quad \text{TreeLike} \iff \forall u v,\ C(u) \cap C(v) = \varnothing \vee C(u) \subseteq C(v) \vee C(v) \subseteq C(u)
candidates.assumptions: Descent is a partial order on forms (u ≤ w means u is an ancestor of w or w itself) in which the ancestors of any form are totally ordered: each form has a single line of ancestry, no hybrid origin between distinct lineages. Groups are clades, the set of all descendants of a founder.
candidates.lean_scope_note: Proves that tree-like descent makes every pair of clades disjoint or nested (groups subordinate to groups), that the clades containing a form are a chain, and conversely that laminarity forces tree-likeness. This is the mathematical core of Darwin's explanation and is not model-dependent beyond the tree assumption. What it does not cover: 'divergence' and 'extinction' play no role (nesting holds with or without them; Darwin invokes them to explain the gaps between groups, which are not formalized), classifications are not proved to be clades (that naturalists' groups coincide with clades is the empirical claim of ch13-02), and reticulate descent (hybridisation, horizontal transfer) violates the hypothesis.

candidates.label: Rarity precedes extinction
candidates.model: integer count falling by at most one per period (gradual decline)
candidates.note: Discrete IVT: the count hits 1 before 0. The hypothesis excludes catastrophic extinction by fiat; this is the thinnest Lean result.
candidates.latex: \forall t,\ N_t \le N_{t+1} + 1;\ N_a \ge 1;\ N_{a+d} = 0 \Rightarrow \exists t \in [a, a+d],\ N_t = 1
candidates.assumptions: The number of individuals of a species (or of species in a group) per period is a natural-number sequence that never falls by more than one per period; the species is present (N ≥ 1) at some period and extinct (N = 0) at a later one.
candidates.lean_scope_note: A discrete intermediate-value argument: under a decline of at most one per period the count must equal 1 (the extreme of rarity) at some period before extinction. Model-dependent in the strongest sense: the hypothesis (no sudden wipe-out) is itself a gradualist premise, and it is exactly what catastrophic extinctions violate, so the theorem cannot distinguish Darwin's view from Cuvier's; it only shows that gradual decline logically entails prior rarity. 'Rare' is rendered as a single survivor, not as Darwin's 'rare' relative to other species; the step size 1 is a normalisation, and any bounded step size with a suitably coarser notion of rarity gives the same result. Darwin's evidence (Tertiary shells, human exterminations) is empirical.

candidates.label: Small genera often grow large while large genera peak, decline and vanish
candidates.model: linear birth–death process per genus (speciation λ, extinction μ)
candidates.note: Not yet formalized. With μ > λ every genus eventually goes extinct, and with λ > 0 any genus has positive probability of reaching any size first; this is the only sense in which 'often' can be derived.
candidates.latex: \text{Linear birth–death from } n_0 = 1:\ \mu \ge \lambda \Rightarrow P(\text{extinction}) = 1;\ \mu < \lambda \Rightarrow P(\text{extinction}) = \mu/\lambda;\ \forall M\ P(\sup_t n(t) \ge M) \ge (\lambda/(\lambda+\mu))^{M-1} > 0
candidates.assumptions: Each species speciates at rate λ and goes extinct at rate μ independently (Kendall 1948); the genus is the lineage count; 'often' is read as positive probability.
candidates.lean_scope_note: A historical pattern that requires extinction and rate heterogeneity: the pure-birth (Yule) model of darwin1859-ch02-15 has no extinction and so no decline, and 'often' is a frequency statement over clades. The discrete rise-and-fall lemma DarwinLaws.Succession.gradual_rise_and_fall assumes the rise and decline rather than deriving them.

candidates.label: Individual differences supply the material for natural selection
candidates.note: Identifies the source of heritable variation; existential statement about populations, not a consequence of premises.
candidates.lean_scope_note: The claim identifies the source of heritable variation that selection acts on; it is a statement about what exists in populations, not a consequence of stated assumptions. The selection dynamics it feeds are formalized under darwin1859-ch04-01 (DarwinLaws.Struggle.selectedFrequency), which takes the existence of a variant with frequency 0 < p < 1 as a hypothesis rather than proving it.

candidates.label: The more ancient a form, the more it differs from living forms
candidates.model: range-through faunas; 'difference' = fewer shared lineages with the living fauna
candidates.note: Weak inequality on shared-lineage counts; not morphological difference.
candidates.latex: i \le j \le \text{now} \Rightarrow |F_i \cap F_{\text{now}}| \le |F_j \cap F_{\text{now}}|,\quad F_t = \{L : \text{first}_L \le t \le \text{last}_L\}
candidates.assumptions: Each lineage has a single stratigraphic range (darwin1859-ch10-04, no reappearance); the fauna of a stage is the set of lineages whose range covers it; 'difference from living forms' is measured by the number of lineages a fauna shares with the living fauna (lower shared count = greater difference).
candidates.lean_scope_note: Proves that an older fauna shares no more lineages with the living fauna than a younger one does (weak inequality). This is a combinatorial consequence of interval ranges and is faithful only if 'differs more' means 'shares fewer lineages'; Darwin's claim is about degree of morphological difference of individual fossil forms, which range-through counting does not measure. The inequality is not strict (two stages can share the same lineages with the present), and the 'as a general rule' is empirical. Darwin's own caveats (living fossils, long-persisting forms) are compatible with the weak inequality.

candidates.label: Overproduction plus slight profitable variation leads to natural selection
candidates.model: geometric increase in a bounded world + constant-fitness haploid selection
candidates.note: Two separate results; the link from overproduction to a fitness difference is not derived.
candidates.latex: N_0 r^t \to \infty\ (r > 1),\ \sup_t N_t \le K \Rightarrow \prod_{i<t} s_i \to 0;\quad w_B < w_A \Rightarrow p' = \frac{p w_A}{p w_A + (1-p) w_B} > p
candidates.assumptions: Overproduction: each generation multiplies numbers by a constant r > 1 and the realised population never exceeds a carrying bound K, with per-generation survival fractions s_t ∈ [0,1]. Selection: a discrete-time, asexual (haploid) population of two types with constant fitnesses w_A > w_B > 0 and initial variant frequency 0 < p₀ < 1.
candidates.lean_scope_note: Two separate results are joined here: (1) under geometric increase in a bounded world the cumulative survival fraction tends to zero, so not every generation can survive in full (the struggle); (2) under a constant fitness advantage the favoured variant increases every generation and its frequency tends to one. Lean proves neither that real fecundity is geometric nor that a 'slight profitable variation' corresponds to a constant fitness difference; it also does not connect the two halves (the struggle does not by itself produce the fitness difference). The inference that selection follows is model-dependent: constant-fitness haploid selection with no drift, mutation, frequency dependence or environmental change.

candidates.label: Keeping large numbers of individuals favours successful selection
candidates.model: same Bernoulli model as ch04-14
candidates.note: Artificial-selection reading of the same theorem.
candidates.latex: P(\text{some favourable variation among } N) = 1 - (1-p)^N,\ \text{strictly increasing in } N,\ \to 1
candidates.assumptions: Each of N individuals independently presents a useful variation with the same probability p, 0 < p < 1.
candidates.lean_scope_note: Proves that the chance of at least one useful variation rises strictly with the number of individuals kept and tends to certainty. Same mathematics as darwin1859-ch04-14, applied to breeders' stock. Independence and a common p are idealisations; the claim's practical conclusion (that large stocks are 'of the highest importance' to breeders, and the breeder's ability to recognise and preserve the variation) is not modelled.

candidates.label: Natural selection preserves favourable and destroys injurious variations
candidates.model: deterministic constant-fitness haploid selection (infinite population, no drift/mutation)
candidates.note: Any advantage raises frequency; constant advantage drives it to one. 'However slight' fails in finite populations.
candidates.latex: p' = \frac{p w_A}{p w_A + (1-p) w_B};\ w_A > w_B \Rightarrow p' > p;\ w_A < w_B \Rightarrow p' < p;\quad p_t = \frac{p_0 w_A^t}{p_0 w_A^t + (1-p_0) w_B^t} \to 1\ (w_A > w_B)
candidates.assumptions: Discrete-time haploid (asexual) selection between a variant with constant fitness w_A and the rest of the population with constant fitness w_B > 0; infinite population (deterministic frequencies), no mutation, no drift, no frequency or density dependence; initial frequency 0 < p₀ < 1.
candidates.lean_scope_note: Proves that any fitness advantage, however slight, raises the variant's frequency in one generation, any disadvantage lowers it, and that under a constant advantage the frequency tends to one so the less favoured type is eliminated. Model-dependent: with finite populations a slight advantage is often lost to drift (the 'however slight' part fails for s ≲ 1/N), with diploid inheritance recessive variants behave differently, and fitnesses in nature are not constant. The claim's causal clause (that this follows from overproduction) is not derived; the fitness difference is assumed. 'Natural selection' is here a name for the recursion, not an empirical process.

candidates.label: Large populations favour natural selection by supplying more variations
candidates.model: independent Bernoulli appearance of a favourable variation with common probability p
candidates.note: Supply of variation only; fixation probability in large populations not treated.
candidates.latex: P_N = 1 - (1-p)^N;\ m < n \Rightarrow P_m < P_n;\ P_N \to 1\ (N \to \infty)
candidates.assumptions: Each of N individuals independently presents a profitable variation in a given period with the same probability p, 0 < p < 1.
candidates.lean_scope_note: Proves that the chance that at least one profitable variation arises in a period rises strictly with population size and tends to one. This is the supply side only; that selection then acts more effectively in large populations (the fixation side, where Kimura's 2s approximation and the drift barrier enter) is not proved. The compensating clause in Darwin's statement, that each individual in a large population is less variable, is not modelled. Independent Bernoulli trials is an idealisation.

candidates.label: Average abundance depends only indirectly on fecundity
candidates.model: stationary population with constant fecundity r and survival s
candidates.note: Only the identity s = 1/r at stationarity. 'Depends only indirectly' is not itself a proposition the identity settles.
candidates.latex: r s N = N,\ N \ne 0 \Rightarrow s = 1/r
candidates.assumptions: A stationary population: N individuals each produce r offspring of which a fraction s survive to breed, and the resulting number r s N equals N; r, N ≠ 0.
candidates.lean_scope_note: Proves only the stationarity identity s = 1/r: in a population of constant average size the survival fraction is the reciprocal of fecundity, so fecundity is exactly compensated by destruction and does not by itself set N. This is a one-line algebraic fact. The claim's substance, that average numbers are set by the checks (destruction, especially early in life) and only indirectly by egg or seed number, is a statement about what determines N, which the identity does not determine; it only shows N is not fixed by r alone. Not an independent theorem of population dynamics.

candidates.label: Varieties form nested groups for the same reason species do
candidates.note: Derivative of ch13-01: the nesting theorem is rank-free, so it applies to varieties. Nothing new is proved.
candidates.latex: \text{TreeLike}(\alpha) \Rightarrow \forall u v,\ C(u) \cap C(v) = \varnothing \vee C(u) \subseteq C(v) \vee C(v) \subseteq C(u),\ \text{for any type } \alpha \text{ of forms}
candidates.assumptions: The same as darwin1859-ch13-01 with the forms taken to be varieties and sub-varieties under a species: descent is a partial order with a single line of ancestry for each form.
candidates.lean_scope_note: The only mathematical content of 'for the same reason' is that the nesting theorem is stated for an arbitrary partially ordered type of forms and so applies to varieties exactly as to species; no separate proof is needed and none is given. It does not prove that domestic or natural varieties actually fall into nested groups (Darwin's observation), nor that their descent is tree-like: domestic breeds are often of hybrid origin, which breaks the hypothesis, and 'various degrees of modification' is not represented. Counts as a theorem only in this derivative sense.

candidates.label: Geometrical increase explains rapid spread of naturalised species
candidates.model: geometric growth with multiplier r·s; lowered mortality s' > s
candidates.note: Shows lowered destruction suffices for rapid (log-time) increase; does not exclude raised fertility.
candidates.latex: \lambda = r s;\ s < s' \Rightarrow r s < r s';\quad \lambda > 1,\ t \ge \frac{\log(M/N_0)}{\log \lambda} \Rightarrow N_0 \lambda^t \ge M
candidates.assumptions: Realised per-generation multiplier λ = r·s with fixed fecundity r > 0 and survival fraction s; in the new country survival is higher (s' > s) because enemies are fewer; growth is geometric with multiplier λ > 1 and target size M ≥ N₀ > 0.
candidates.lean_scope_note: Proves that at fixed fecundity higher survival gives a strictly higher multiplier, and that a geometrically growing population reaches any size M within log(M/N₀)/log λ generations ('extraordinarily rapid' read as logarithmic time). It does not prove that naturalised species spread because of lowered mortality rather than raised fertility: the alternative (a rise in r) is not shown to be absent, only that lowered destruction suffices. The model has no spatial spread, density dependence or lag phase.

candidates.label: Extinct species are often intermediate between living groups
candidates.model: nonnegative path-additive (tree) metric on character space
candidates.note: Common ancestor is metrically between descendants; immediate from additivity. Most extinct species are not ancestors.
candidates.latex: d(x,y) = d(x,a) + d(a,y),\ a = \mathrm{lca}(x,y),\ d \ge 0 \Rightarrow d(x,a) \le d(x,y) \wedge d(a,y) \le d(x,y)
candidates.assumptions: Character distance between forms is a nonnegative path-additive (tree) metric: the distance between two forms equals the sum of their distances to their last common ancestor. 'Intermediate in character' is read as metric betweenness of that ancestor.
candidates.lean_scope_note: Model-dependent (tree metric) and mathematically slight: given additivity and nonnegativity the conclusion is immediate. Proves that the common ancestor of two living groups is no farther from either than they are from each other. It does not prove that extinct species in general are such ancestors (most are side branches), that character change is additive along lineages (convergence and reversal break this), or the 'often' in Darwin's wording, which is the empirical content and is left to data.

candidates.label: Divergence of character maximises the life an area supports
candidates.model: additive resource partition: life supported = Σ K_i over resources used
candidates.note: Unused resources mean strictly less life. Does not show diversification covers more resources or that selection produces it.
candidates.latex: L(U) = \sum_{i \in U} K_i,\ K_i > 0;\quad U \subsetneq I \Rightarrow L(U) < L(I);\quad A \subseteq B \Rightarrow L(A) \le L(B)
candidates.assumptions: The area's resources ('places in the economy of nature') form a finite set, each resource i alone supporting K_i > 0 units of life; the life supported by an assemblage is the sum of K_i over the resources its species' niches cover (additive partition, no interaction between resources, no cost of specialisation).
candidates.lean_scope_note: Model-dependent (additive resource partition). Proves that an assemblage leaving some resource unused supports strictly less life than one covering every resource, and that adding a species whose niche includes an unused resource strictly increases the total. 'Diversification of structure' is identified with covering more resource classes; the theorem does not show that diversified assemblages cover more resources than uniform ones, nor that selection produces divergence (the mechanism half of Darwin's principle of divergence). Darwin's supporting evidence (Lamb and grass-plot experiments, naturalised floras) is empirical.

candidates.label: The Natural System expresses propinquity of descent
candidates.note: A claim about what classifications track; showing that resemblance-based groups recover clades is phylogenetic-inference theory under a character model, not a proposition in Darwin's text.
candidates.lean_scope_note: A claim about what naturalists' classifications track; it identifies the 'something more' of the Natural System with genealogy. Formally one would have to show that a classification built from resemblances recovers clades, which depends on how characters evolve and is the subject of phylogenetic-inference theory, not of anything in the module. DarwinLaws.Tree.clade_laminar gives the nesting that descent produces, not that resemblance-based groups are clades.

candidates.label: Favoured forms make less favoured forms rare, and rarity precedes extinction
candidates.model: constant-fitness selection (first half) + unit-step decline in numbers (second half)
candidates.note: Frequency decline read as rarity; 'fully stocked' premise not modelled.
candidates.latex: w_A < w_B \Rightarrow p' < p,\ p_t \to 0\ \text{(less favoured)};\quad N_t \le N_{t+1} + 1,\ N_a \ge 1,\ N_{a+d} = 0 \Rightarrow \exists t \in [a, a+d],\ N_t = 1
candidates.assumptions: First half: constant-fitness haploid selection as in darwin1859-ch04-01, the less favoured form having fitness w_A < w_B, so its frequency falls every generation and the favoured form's tends to one. Second half: the count of individuals of the less favoured form falls by at most one per period (no instantaneous wipe-out).
candidates.lean_scope_note: Two halves from two models. Selection: the less favoured variant's frequency decreases monotonically and tends to zero, which is read as 'becomes rare'; this is frequency, not number, and the full-stocking premise ('every area is already fully stocked', which is what turns a frequency change into a decline in numbers) is not modelled. Rarity before extinction: given a decline of at most one individual per period, the count must pass through 1. The unit-step hypothesis does the work and excludes catastrophic extinction by assumption; see darwin1859-ch10-09. Neither half is an empirical result.

candidates.label: Species of larger genera more often present varieties
candidates.note: Tabulation result about the proportion of varying species; a constant per-species rate gives no such effect, and a size-dependent rate assumes it.
candidates.lean_scope_note: Darwin's statement is about the proportion of species that vary and the mean number of varieties per varying species. In the constant-rate pure-birth model used for darwin1859-ch02-15 every species produces varieties at the same rate, so the per-species proportion is the same in large and small genera; only the absolute number scales with genus size (DarwinLaws.Tree.expectedGain_proportional). A model in which the per-species rate rises with genus size would assume the claim. It is a tabulation result (Darwin's own tables), left to data.

candidates.label: Struggle is most severe between members of the same species
candidates.model: MacArthur–Levins niche overlap (cosine similarity of utilisation vectors)
candidates.note: Cauchy–Schwarz: self-overlap is maximal. Nearly a tautology of the chosen measure; weak inequality.
candidates.latex: \alpha(u,v) = \frac{\sum_i u_i v_i}{\sqrt{\sum_i u_i^2}\sqrt{\sum_i v_i^2}};\quad \alpha(u,u) = 1,\ \alpha(u,v) \le \alpha(u,u)
candidates.assumptions: Competition intensity between two forms is their MacArthur–Levins competition coefficient, the cosine similarity of their resource-utilisation vectors over a finite set of resource classes; both vectors are nonzero; members of one species share a single utilisation vector.
candidates.lean_scope_note: Model-dependent (MacArthur–Levins niche overlap). Proves by Cauchy–Schwarz that no other form's overlap with a given form exceeds its self-overlap, which is 1. This is close to a tautology of the chosen measure: any normalised inner-product similarity is maximised on the diagonal, so the theorem says nothing about real competition unless one already accepts that utilisation similarity is what makes the struggle severe. It does not prove the 'almost always' in Darwin's wording, does not treat intraspecific variation in resource use (which would make α(u,u) a within-species average less than 1), and does not model non-resource competition (mates, predators, disease). The ≤ is not strict: a different form with a proportional utilisation vector competes just as hard.

candidates.label: Congeners compete more severely than species of different genera
candidates.note: Within the niche-overlap model it reduces to 'congeners have more similar utilisation vectors', an empirical premise.
candidates.lean_scope_note: Within the niche-overlap model of darwin1859-ch03-11, the claim becomes 'congeners have more similar utilisation vectors than non-congeners', which is an empirical premise about how resource use is distributed on the phylogeny, not a consequence of anything proved. Adding it as a hypothesis would make the theorem restate its assumption.

candidates.label: The closest-competing neighbours tend to belong to different genera and orders
candidates.note: Taxonomic composition of small plots; no derivation from stated premises without assuming genera map to resources.
candidates.lean_scope_note: An empirical pattern about the taxonomic composition of small plots. The additive-partition model of darwin1859-ch04-20 explains why covering more resources supports more life, but says nothing about taxonomy; turning 'different genera use different resources' into a hypothesis would make the conclusion a restatement.

candidates.label: Larger genera tend to grow larger and dominant forms more dominant
candidates.model: Yule pure-birth process, expectations only
candidates.note: Absolute gap grows; ratio of expected sizes is constant, so no relative advantage. Truth score 0.4 agrees the claim says more than the model gives.
candidates.latex: \mathbb{E}[n(t)] = n_0 e^{\lambda t};\ \mathbb{E}[n(t)] - n_0 = n_0(e^{\lambda t} - 1);\ \frac{\mathbb{E}[n_1(t)]}{\mathbb{E}[n_2(t)]} = \frac{n_1}{n_2};\quad n_1 > n_2,\ \lambda > 0 \Rightarrow (n_1 - n_2)e^{\lambda t} \text{ strictly increasing in } t
candidates.assumptions: Yule's pure-birth process (1925, built for this very claim): every species in every genus gives rise to new species at the same constant rate λ > 0, with no extinction; only expected sizes n₀ e^{λt} are treated, not the stochastic process.
candidates.lean_scope_note: Model-dependent (Yule pure birth, expectations only). Proves that the expected gain of a genus is proportional to its size, that two genera with the same rate keep a constant ratio of expected sizes, and that the absolute gap between a larger and a smaller genus grows strictly with time. It does not prove 'dominant forms become more dominant' in any sense beyond this absolute gap: the ratio is constant, so no relative advantage accrues, and Darwin's mechanism (dominant species vary more and their varieties become species) is replaced by a uniform rate that gives large genera no per-species edge. With extinction or rate heterogeneity (ch02-09) large genera can shrink. The data test for this claim is pending; the truth score is low (0.4), which is consistent with the theorem proving less than the claim says.
